lesson.title: Smart in Different Ways? Gardner's Theory of Multiple Intelligences
lesson.summary: Howard Gardner proposed that intelligence is really several distinct capacities rather than one general factor, a theory influential in education but only weakly supported by psychometric testing.
lesson.body:
If Spearman's g represents intelligence as one general capacity that shows up across every mental task, Howard Gardner's theory of multiple intelligences represents almost the opposite instinct. In his 1983 book Frames of Mind, Gardner argued that what people casually call intelligence is really a collection of several distinct, relatively independent capacities, each rooted in different patterns of brain organization and each valuable in different areas of life. His original list included linguistic, logical mathematical, spatial, musical, bodily kinesthetic, interpersonal, and intrapersonal intelligences, and he later added naturalistic intelligence and discussed other candidates, such as existential intelligence, without fully committing to them as a finished, closed list.

Gardner's case rested less on traditional psychometric testing, of the kind Spearman and later intelligence researchers relied on, and more on evidence drawn from neuroscience, child development, and case studies of specific talents and impairments. He pointed, for example, to individuals who show remarkable ability in one narrow domain, such as music or spatial reasoning, alongside more ordinary or even impaired performance elsewhere, arguing that a single unitary g factor struggles to explain such uneven profiles.

The theory has had an enormous and lasting influence on education. Teachers and curriculum designers have used it to justify presenting material through multiple formats, combining visual, verbal, and hands on activities, and to push back against the idea that a single test score can capture everything worthwhile about a student's abilities. This is one of the theory's genuine strengths: it broadened how many educators think about talent and capability beyond narrow academic measures.

It is important, though, to represent the scientific standing of the theory fairly rather than treating it as settled fact. When researchers have tried to test Gardner's proposed intelligences using the same factor analytic methods that support g, the results have generally not supported the idea that these are truly separate, statistically independent abilities. Measures of Gardner's different intelligences tend to correlate with each other and with general measures of g more than his theory would predict if they were fully distinct. Critics have also noted that some of the proposed intelligences, such as musical or bodily kinesthetic ability, look more like specific talents or skills than intelligences in the traditional psychological sense, and that the criteria for what counts as a distinct intelligence have been applied somewhat flexibly.

None of this means the theory is worthless. It remains a useful, influential framework for thinking about the many forms human competence can take, and it has real educational value as a way of broadening what counts as ability in a classroom. But as a scientific account of the structure of intelligence, it sits in tension with, rather than replacing, the psychometric evidence for a general factor, and this tension between a broad, humanistic view of talent and a narrower, statistically supported view of general cognitive ability is one of the more genuinely unresolved debates in this area of psychology.
